meta.title: Who really said "Government is not reason, it is not eloquence, it is force; like fire, a troublesome servant and a fearful master"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — George Washington never said it. This line first surfaced in 1902, a century after his death, and Mount Vernon lists it as spurious. Here is the real trail.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Government is not reason, it is not eloquence, it is force; like fire, a troublesome servant and a fearful master'?
meta.ogDescription: George Washington never said it. The line first appears in a 1902 magazine, 103 years after his death. Mount Vernon calls it spurious. The real trail, verified.

answer.label: Not George Washington — a spurious quotation
answer.authorDates: 1732–1799 · First U.S. president; no evidence he said this
answer.sourceLine: There is no record of Washington ever saying or writing this. The phrasing first appears in print in 1902 — more than a century after his death — and researchers, including the editor of the Yale Book of Quotations, have found it in none of Washington’s writings ↗. Washington’s own estate at Mount Vernon lists it among its “spurious quotations.”

source.heading: The 1902 trail, not a Washington manuscript

docMeta.dd: “Liberty and Government,” The Christian Science Journal, Vol. XX, No. 8 (Nov. 1902)
Spurious — no evidence in Washington’s writings

source.excerpt: Government is not reason, it is not eloquence,—it is force! Like fire, it is a dangerous servant, and a fearful master; never for a moment should it be left to irresponsible action.
trail: 1799: George Washington dies, leaving no known text containing this line — Eugene Volokh checked the Farewell Address and the sources where it is often claimed to originate; “it’s not in either” ↗.
1902: the earliest documented appearance, in The Christian Science Journal, crediting only “the first President of the United States” ↗ — 103 years after Washington’s death.
1915: Upton Sinclair reprints it in The Cry for Justice, from which it spread widely ↗.
Today: the editor of the Yale Book of Quotations notes “no one has ever found any evidence that Washington said it ↗.”
source.excerptNote: The wording as it first appeared in The Christian Science Journal (1902), where it was credited only to “the first President of the United States.” Popular modern versions swap “dangerous servant” for “troublesome servant” and trim the closing clause — no version traces to Washington himself.

source.rightsNote: The wording is of unknown authorship — it first surfaces anonymously in an 1902 magazine and cannot be tied to Washington or any identified writer, so no reliable public-domain claim can be asserted for it as a Washington quotation. The 1902 Christian Science Journal text itself is old enough to be in the public domain, but the line is not Washington’s.

author.name: George Washington
author.heading: About the man it’s pinned on
author.metaLine: 1732–1799 · First President of the United States · Commander of the Continental Army
author.bio: George Washington led the Continental Army to victory in the American Revolution and served as the first U.S. president from 1789 to 1797. His genuine writings — including the Farewell Address — are extensively documented, which is precisely why researchers can say with confidence that this anti-government aphorism appears nowhere in them. The line was attached to his name only in the 20th century.

misattribution.heading: How a 1902 line became a Washington quote
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely circulated fake founding-father quotes. The attribution has no 18th-century footing whatsoever.

items.why: No variant of this line appears in Washington’s writings. Fred Shapiro, editor of the Yale Book of Quotations: “No one has ever found any evidence that Washington said it” ↗, and Mount Vernon lists it as spurious.
A popular claim sources the line to an early Washington-era newspaper. Volokh checked that issue and the Farewell Address: “It’s not in either” ↗.
The “servant / master” frame long predates him — fire was called “a good servant but a bad master” as early as the 1600s ↗; the government application only surfaces in 1902.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest known appearance is an anonymous 1902 magazine article; the line was pinned on Washington posthumously and is now on Mount Vernon’s own list of quotes he never said ↗.

context.heading: Why this one spreads
lead: The quote is potent political rhetoric — a stark, quotable warning about state power — and Washington’s name lends it unimpeachable authority. That combination is exactly what makes fabricated founder quotes travel so far.
Its real lineage runs through an old “good servant, bad master” proverb, reworked into an anti-government epigram that first appears, unsigned, in 1902 and was popularized by Upton Sinclair in 1915.
context.pull: “No one has ever found any evidence that Washington said it.”
